title: The Mozart effect
hook: A brief boost on one puzzle became a myth that Mozart makes babies smarter.
peek: A 1993 study found college students did slightly better on a spatial task for a few minutes after hearing Mozart. Within a few years the idea had become 'music makes babies smarter', and one US state planned to give every newborn a classical CD.
lede: In 1993, Frances Rauscher, Gordon Shaw and Katherine Ky reported in Nature that 36 college students scored better on a spatial reasoning test after ten minutes of a Mozart sonata. The boost was small and faded within about 15 minutes. Nobody tested babies or general intelligence. Even so, it grew into a popular belief that classical music makes children cleverer.

bullets.text: The piece was Mozart's Sonata for Two Pianos in D major, K. 448. Students compared it with relaxation instructions and silence, then did spatial puzzles from an IQ test, such as imagining how a folded, cut sheet would look once opened.

In 1998, the governor of Georgia proposed spending about $105,000 a year so that every baby born in the state could go home with a classical music CD. Tennessee had a similar scheme, and products for babies multiplied.

Many labs could not repeat the effect, and reviews found any boost was small. Psychologist Glenn Schellenberg showed it fits a simpler story: music people enjoy lifts mood and alertness, which briefly helps on tasks like this.

In a 1996 study run with the BBC, more than 8,000 British schoolchildren took part. Those who heard pop music from Blur and other bands did slightly better on a spatial task than those who heard Mozart. The music they liked mattered more than the composer.
